title: Chapter 86 — The Delivered Base: Repeat Business and The Replacement Cycle
intro: Every appliance has a lifespan. Every customer has a household full of appliances. The replacement cycle is the pipeline that builds itself — if you track it.

sections.title: Your Past Customers Are Your Future Sales
sections.content:
Every sale you have ever made represents a future sale. A washer bought today will need replacing in 8 to 12 years. A refrigerator in 10 to 15 years. A range in 13 to 18 years.

If you track what every customer bought and when, your CRM becomes a prediction engine. You know who is approaching the end of their appliance's life. You know who will be shopping before they know it themselves.

That is not aggressive selling. That is proactive service. A check-in message at year seven of a washer's life is helpful — not pushy.

sections.title: Lifetime Value Thinking
sections.content:
A single customer is not a single sale. A homeowner may buy appliances for their kitchen, their laundry room, their basement, their rental property, their vacation home, and their next house.

Over a lifetime, one satisfied customer can generate $15,000 to $25,000 in purchases — plus every referral they send your way.

When you see each customer as a lifetime relationship instead of a one-time transaction, everything about how you sell changes. You stop chasing the quick close and start building the long relationship. The math favours the long relationship every time.

sections.title: Mining the Base
sections.content:
Once a quarter, review your CRM for customers whose appliances are approaching replacement age. A simple message can reopen the relationship.

'Your dishwasher is coming up on eight years. These models typically start needing attention around this age. If you are noticing any issues, I am happy to help you explore options before it becomes an emergency.'

That is genuine service. And it positions you as the first call when they are ready.

sections.title: The Post-Sale Touchpoint Calendar
content: Step 11 of selling is the step most salespeople skip — and it's the one that builds careers. After the delivery, after the install, after the dust settles — that's when the real relationship begins.

**The 48-Hour Check-In Call.** Two days after delivery, call the customer. Not to sell. Not to survey. Just to ask: 'How's everything working? Anything I can help with?' This single call does more for your reputation than any marketing campaign. Most customers have never received a post-delivery call from a salesperson. You'll be the first. They'll remember.

**The 30-Day Follow-Up.** A month in, send a quick email or text. 'Just checking in — how are you enjoying the new kitchen?' By now they've cooked in it, done laundry in it, lived with it. If there's an issue, you catch it before it becomes a complaint. If everything's great, you've just reinforced that buying from you was the right decision.

**Anniversary Cards.** One year after their purchase, send a card. Physical mail, not email. 'Happy anniversary with your new kitchen — hope you're still loving it.' This is shockingly rare in retail. The customer will tell people about it. It costs you a stamp and 30 seconds.

**Holiday Cards.** A simple holiday card to your delivered base every December. Not a sales pitch. Not a coupon. Just a card from you. 'Happy holidays from [your name] at [your store].' Your delivered base is your farm. Holiday cards are how you tend it.

**The Replacement Cycle Alert.** Appliances have predictable lifespans. A dishwasher bought 8 years ago is approaching replacement age. A washer from 10 years ago is on borrowed time. Track purchase dates and reach out when the replacement window opens: 'Your Whirlpool washer is about 9 years old — if it's starting to show its age, I'd love to help you look at what's new.' This is not cold calling. This is informed, welcome outreach to someone who already trusts you.

**The Referral Ask.** Every touchpoint is a soft referral opportunity. Not aggressive — just present. 'If anyone you know is shopping for appliances, I'd love to help them the same way.' Said naturally at the end of a check-in call, this generates more referrals than any formal referral program.
Most salespeople think the sale ends at delivery. Career salespeople know the sale begins at delivery. Step 11 is what separates a salesperson from a sales career.

sections.title: Coaching Rule
sections.content:
When evaluating base management, ask:

Does the salesperson track what each customer bought and when?
Do they proactively reach out to customers approaching replacement cycles?
Do they think in terms of lifetime value — or single transactions?
Is their CRM a living tool — or a dead database?

The salesperson who manages their delivered base never runs out of pipeline.
